outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in Adjectives and adverbs.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.

key_terms.definition: A lexical category whose members typically modify nouns and denote properties.
A lexical category whose members characteristically modify verbs and other categories except nouns.
The function of an adjective phrase used as a pre-head modifier inside a nominal.
A complement that ascribes a property to a predicand, often realised by an AdjP.
The function of an adjective phrase used as a post-head modifier inside an NP.
Able to denote a property in varying degrees, as with happy, happier, very happy.
A use of an adjective that does not readily accept degree modification or comparison.
An adverb such as very, too, quite or enough that indicates the degree of a property.
The grade form used to compare two or more entities, as in happier or more useful.
The grade form used to single out the highest degree, as in happiest or most useful.
A phrase headed by an adjective, with optional modifiers and complements.
A phrase headed by an adverb, with optional modifiers and complements.
A dependent licensed by the head, such as of dogs in afraid of dogs.
A dependent that adds information without being required by the head.
An adjective restricted to attributive function, such as former or mere.
An adjective excluded from attributive function, such as asleep or alone.
An adverb with the same form as an adjective, such as fast or hard.
A modifier in clause structure, such as a manner or time expression.
An adjunct that modifies the predicate, such as manner or frequency.
An adjunct that modifies the clause’s applicability, such as evaluation or modality.
An adverb such as only or also that highlights a particular constituent.
The element that a focusing modifier applies to semantically.
A sequence in which one modifier is itself modified, as in only very rarely.
A structure in which a modifier modifies another modifier, as in quite remarkably well.

options.feedback: Adjectives modify nominals and denote properties.
Adverbs characteristically modify categories other than nouns.
Prepositions head PPs; they do not modify nouns in this way.

opening.prompt: Which function is a predicative adjective performing?

options.text: Acting as a complement that ascribes a property
options.feedback: In She is happy, happy is a predicative complement.
That is the attributive function.
Prepositions head PPs.
The child was asleep, but not an asleep child in ordinary use.
Happy occurs attributively and predicatively.
Former is attributive-only.

opening.prompt: What does an adverb characteristically modify?

options.text: Verbs and categories other than nouns
options.feedback: Adverbs also modify adjectives, adverbs, PPs and clauses.
That is the adjective’s characteristic function.
Adverbs also modify adjectives, adverbs, PPs and clauses.

opening.prompt: What does a focusing adverb highlight?

options.feedback: Only in Only Kim resigned highlights Kim.
A focus selects a particular element within the scope.
Focusing adverbs can modify many categories.

closing.prompt: Why is of dogs a complement in afraid of dogs?

options.feedback: The adjective’s lexical entry selects the preposition.
Position alone does not determine complement status.
Optional complements are still licensed.

closing.prompt: Where does enough normally occur with an adjective?

options.feedback: Old enough, not enough old.
Enough old is not the normal order.
Enough has its own placement rules.
Utter nonsense, but not The nonsense is utter in ordinary use.
Awake is never-attributive.
Happy occurs in all three central functions.

closing.prompt: Why is outside a preposition in They are outside?

options.text: It heads a PP and can occur as a complement of be.
options.feedback: The category is based on syntax, not the traditional label.
It is a complement, not a modifier.
Morphology alone does not decide.

closing.prompt: Why does Happily, they watched TV differ from They happily watched TV?

options.text: Front position gives an evaluation reading; central position gives a manner reading.
options.feedback: Position affects scope and orientation.

options.text: Happily is an adjective in the first sentence.
options.feedback: It is an adverb in both.

options.text: The second sentence has no subject.
options.feedback: They is the subject.
